title: Node isolation & soft failover playbook (draft)
body:
Purpose:
This draft defines a 'soft failover' play for infra failures where we isolate an unhealthy node (node-level GPU/cable/host issues) and route traffic away while keeping overall latency SLOs by enabling a temporary degraded service path (CPU/quantized-variant pool or regional fallback). The goal: minimize user-visible errors, preserve KV cache where possible, and perform rolling backfill (replace capacity) with minimal disruption.

Scope and when to use this playbook:
- Partial hardware degradation (GPU ECC spikes, intermittent GPU driver OOMs, HOST_STORAGE_READ_ERRORS) that cause >5% error rate or >20ms p50 token latency regression for a route for >5 minutes.
- Node shows kernel oops, repeated kubelet restarts, or GPU unreachable events but the rest of cluster healthy.
- NOT for full-region outage or control-plane failure (use multi-region failover playbook).

Key concepts (soft failover):
1) Soft traffic diversion: create a temporary, lower-cost fallback path (CPU-only or smaller-quantized model variant) and shift a fraction of traffic for affected routes (canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%) until capacity replacement ready.
2) Node isolation: cordon -> drain (graceful) but prefer preserving cache where critical by draining non-cache-critical pods first and using pod-priority/taints to move reproducers.
3) Rolling backfill: incrementally add replacement GPU-backed nodes, label/taint them, let scheduler place pods, and warm KV/cache before shifting traffic back.

Quick checklist (first 10 mins):
- Acknowledge in #sre-oncall and create an incident channel: #incident-<date>-<runid>.
- Capture run id: incident-run: <YYYYMMDD>-sre-<3digit>.
- Post immediate airway: what is impacted (routes/models), basic metrics (error rate, p50/p95), any alerts firing.
- Confirm if the problem is local to a node: kubectl get nodes, check AGE/STATUS, kubectl describe node <node> for recent events.

Signals to act on node isolation:
- GPU driver disconnects or repeated "GPU unreachable" events in dmesg/syslog.
- kubelet restarts >2x in 10m or NodeCondition MemoryPressure/NetworkUnavailable.
- Pod OOMKill on inference pods only on that node but not others.

Immediate commands (keep in notes log):
- Get node state: kubectl get node <node> -o wide
- Recent events: kubectl describe node <node> | sed -n '1,240p'
- Pods on node: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- GPU metrics: ssh gpu-host and run nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,UTILIZATION,DRIVER
- Start incident log: echo "incident-run:<id> node:<node> start:$(date -u)" >> /var/log/sre/incident-logs.txt

Soft isolation steps (recommended sequence):
1) Create degraded-route target(s):
   - If not existing, create a CPU/quantized model deployment (name: <route>-degraded-<runid>) with lower memory reqs and lower concurrency. Use existing job template for cpu-fallback.
   - Expose the degraded deployment behind the same API route via the routing layer as a secondary backend.
2) Shift traffic policy:
   - Update route rollout policy in Console or via API to divert 10% traffic to degraded path. Monitor for errors and latency. (Use canary key: "soft-failover-<runid>").
   - After 10m and stable, increase to 50% if primary still degraded; use 1-minute rollout windows.
3) Cordon the node(s): kubectl cordon <node> # prevents new pods
4) Drain non-critical pods first:
   - Annotate pods that we want to keep on-node temporarily (cache-warm pods) with: kubectl annotate pod <pod> preserve-cache="true" 
   - Evict inference-sidecars and stateless frontends first: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='!preserve-cache' --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
   - For pods annotated preserve-cache=true, we can choose to leave them until replacements are ready (see section on cache warming).
5) Monitor workloads moving off node: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -w
6) If drain stalls (Eviction stuck >10m), escalate:
   - Check PDBs: kubectl get pdb -n <ns> and assess. If safe, bypass PDBs with --force (last resort).
   - Check for local PVs blocking delete: kubectl describe pod <pod> and check volumes.

Rolling backfill & replacement steps:
- If the underlying host is healthy enough for repair (e.g., GPU reseated), coordinate with infra-ops for a physical swap. Otherwise start an automated replacement:
  1) Increase node pool desired count by +1 in the autoscaler group (Terraform/Cloud console). Tag new nodes with label replacement-for=<old-node> and taint node:gpu-ready=false until image + drivers validated.
  2) Once new node up, run preflight: ssh to node, check nvidia-smi, docker runtimes, kernel modules. Add label node.k8s.io/gpu=true and remove taint gpu-ready=false to allow scheduling.
  3) Allow scheduler to place pods; monitor pod status. Warm KV cache: run a short synthetic workload to populate model KV caches (script location: infra/scripts/cache_warm.sh).
  4) When new node warmed and inference latencies stable, progressively shift traffic back from degraded path to primary (10% steps).

KV/cache considerations:
- Aim to preserve larger KV caches; when draining, prioritize eviction order to keep cache-holding pods running on replacement nodes if possible.
- Use cache-warm jobs targeting the model variant and prefix used by traffic. Document the warm duration: typically 2–5 minutes per model depending on seq length.

Fallback decisions and SLO thresholds:
- If degraded path latency is within SLO+20% and error rate <1% after 30m, keep degraded path for up to 8 hours while replacement completed.
- If degraded path errors >1% or p95 > 2x baseline, escalate to full circuit (route failover to multi-region).

When to perform immediate evacuation (hard):
- Node is flapping control plane or reported disk pressure that will impact many pods.
- Host indicates hardware burnout (thermal shutdowns) or smoke alarms (escalate to physical ops immediately).

Post-action recovery and cleanup:
- After replacement and traffic shift complete: kubectl uncordon <old-node> (if old node will be returned to service) OR mark node for decommission: kubectl drain <node> --delete-local-data --force; then remove from pool in infra console.
- Remove temporary degraded deployments and routing rules: console rollback or API remove: route.removeFallback("soft-failover-<runid>")
- Capture incident notes: root cause hypothesis, timeline, mitigations, and action items. Add to CONFLUENCE: SRE Incident Reviews with tag: gpu-failures.

Postmortem checklist (required if incident >30m or customer impact):
- Timeline (UTC) with actor and commands.
- Root cause: (hardware/drivers/kernel/config/bug).
- What worked: list mitigations that reduced user impact.
- Action items with owners and ETA.
- Rollout prevention plan for similar future events (monitoring, autoscaler tuning, new taints).

Runbook TODOs and open questions (draft items):
- [ ] Add exact Console API call examples for traffic diversion.
- [ ] Create standardized degraded deployment template per model family.
- [ ] Add automation to auto-create degraded path when GPU error rate spikes.
- [ ] Define exact error-rate thresholds per route (currently uses global heuristics).

References and useful commands (copyable):
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,UTILIZATION,DRIVER
- terraform apply -target=module.node_pool -var 'desired_size=+1' (replace with infra-specific invocation)
- curl -X POST "https://console.redwood/api/routes/<route>/rollout" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"policy":"soft-failover","weights":{"primary":90,"degraded":10}}'

Notes to oncall (voice-of-author):
- Prefer preserving cache pods for heavy models; losing KV cache often costs more tokens/latency than serving a slightly slower CPU-based fallback.
- Never escalate PDB bypass without communicating to owners in the incident channel.
- Keep the degraded path as explicit and labeled: name it soft-failover-<runid> so cleanup is straightforward.

Revision history:
- v0.1 (2025-11-03) initial draft by Priya K.
- v0.2 (2026-01-08) added cache warming and traffic policy details (Ethan M.)
- v0.3 (2026-02-20) clarified drain sequence and added automation TODOs (Lina A.)

End of draft.
